title: Game State and Save Files
summary: Saving a game means deciding what state matters, writing it in a format that will still load after the game is updated, and never leaving a corrupted file behind. This lesson covers what to save and what to rebuild, binary and text formats, **versioning** and migrating old saves, **checksums** that detect damage, and writing files safely.
markdown:
## What to save A running game holds far more state than needs saving. Divide it: | Save | Rebuild on load | Do not save | |---|---|---| | The player's position, stats, inventory, quest flags | Anything derived: collision grids, pathfinding data, cached totals | Pointers and handles (lesson 6.09): they mean nothing next time | | What has changed in the world: opened chests, killed bosses | Static level content: it comes from the level file | Rendering state, GPU resources | | Settings the player chose | | Temporary effects that do not matter | A useful principle: **save the minimum from which everything else can be rebuilt**. Small saves are fast to write, and less saved state means fewer ways for a save to be inconsistent. References between saved objects (a quest that refers to an NPC) are saved as **ids**, and resolved back to objects after loading, never as pointers. ## Binary or text | | Binary | Text (JSON, INI, your own) | |---|---|---| | Size and speed | Small and fast | Larger and slower to parse | | Readable by people | No | Yes: easy to inspect and debug | | Robust to change | Needs explicit versioning | Easier to add fields (unknown keys can be ignored) | | Editable by players | Hard | Easy, which may or may not be wanted | Many games use text during development and binary when shipping, or text for settings and binary for saves. Whichever you choose, write fields individually in a defined byte order (lesson 2.06), never by dumping structs from memory: padding, pointers and compiler differences would all leak into the file. ## A header with a version Every save file should start with a small fixed header: ```cpp // Written field by field, little-endian, 16 bytes: // magic 4 bytes 'S','A','V','E' what kind of file this is // version 4 bytes format version how to read the rest // length 4 bytes bytes after the header // checksum 4 bytes CRC-32 of those bytes ``` - The **magic** number rejects files that are not saves at all. - The **version** lets the game read old formats after updates. - The **checksum** detects corruption: truncated writes, disk errors, a file damaged in transfer. ## Versioning and migration Games change after release, and players expect their saves to keep working. The usual approach: each format version gets a loader, and old versions are **migrated** step by step to the current one: ```mermaid flowchart LR V1["version 1 file"] -->|"migrate 1→2:
add 'gold', default 0"| V2["version 2 data"] V2 -->|"migrate 2→3:
split 'name' into first/last"| V3["version 3 data
(current)"] ``` Each migration is small and tested once, and a save from any old version passes through all of them. Never reuse a version number for a different layout, and keep test saves from every released version so you can check old saves still load. ## Checksums A **checksum** is a number computed from all the bytes, stored alongside them. On loading, recompute it; if it differs, the data is damaged. **CRC-32** is the standard choice: it catches accidental corruption (bit flips, truncation, garbage) with very high probability, and it is cheap. The practice task implements it. A CRC detects **accidents**, not deliberate tampering: anyone who edits a save can recompute it. Preventing cheating in a single-player game is rarely worth it; in multiplayer, anything that matters must live on the server, not in a file on the player's machine. ## Writing safely Lesson 5.04's technique applies fully: write the whole save to a temporary file, flush it, then atomically replace the old save. Keeping the previous save as a backup (`slot1.sav.bak`) as well means even a save that was written correctly but contains a game bug can be recovered. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Dumping structs to disk with `fwrite(&state, sizeof state, ...)` > Padding, pointers and layout differences make the file fragile and unportable. Write fields one by one. > [!warning] No version number > The first update that changes the format breaks every existing save. > [!warning] Overwriting the save in place > A crash mid-write destroys it. Write a temporary file and replace. > [!warning] Trusting the file > A save may be damaged or edited. Check the magic, the version, the checksum and every length before using the data. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What should a save contain, and what should be rebuilt? - Everything in memory, so loading is a single copy + Only state that cannot be derived; the rest is rebuilt on load - Only the level number; everything else is reset - The game's code and its data, so the save works on any version > Saving derived data wastes space and risks it disagreeing with what it was derived from. ? What goes in a save file's header? - The player's name and the date only - The compiled code needed to read the file + A magic number, a version, a length and a checksum - The pointers of every saved object > The magic number and version say how to read the rest; the length and checksum detect truncated or damaged files. ? How do old saves keep working after the format changes? - The game refuses old saves and asks the player to start again - Old saves are read with the newest loader, ignoring any differences - The game stores every save in every format at once + Each version is migrated step by step up to the current one > Each migration step only needs to know about two neighbouring versions. ? Why are references between saved objects stored as ids rather than pointers? + Addresses differ the next time the game runs - Ids are smaller - Pointers cannot be written to files > ASLR and new allocations change every address between runs. ? What is a save file's version number for? - Showing the player which save is newest + Telling the loader which format the file uses - Detecting corruption > Each format change gets a new version and a migration from the old one. ? What does a CRC-32 checksum detect? - Deliberate editing by the player - Which version of the game wrote the file + Accidental damage to the data, such as truncation or flipped bits > Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is not tamper protection. ```
ideas:
- Design the save format for the game you will build in chapter 11: list the fields, their types and sizes.
- Write a save, change one byte in a hex editor, and check that your loader rejects it.
- Write a version 2 of your format with one extra field and a migration from version 1.

cards.q: What should a save contain, and what should be rebuilt?
cards.a:
Only state that cannot be derived; the rest is rebuilt on load

Saving derived data wastes space and risks it disagreeing with what it was derived from.

cards.q: What goes in a save file's header?

cards.a:
Each version is migrated step by step up to the current one

Each migration step only needs to know about two neighbouring versions.

cards.a:

ASLR and new allocations change every address between runs.

cards.a:
Telling the loader which format the file uses

Each format change gets a new version and a migration from the old one.

cards.a:
Accidental damage to the data, such as truncation or flipped bits

Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is not tamper protection.
